records.name: Yozgat
records.current_summary: No Yozgat-specific trans statute, enforcement series or incident pattern was found in this pass; the province sits in the dossier's 'no sub-national signal' group, with the standing caveat that here absence of documentation means absence of local divergence — not evidence of local safety. What applies in full is the country-wide picture documented by the three sources: a leaked October 2025 judicial package would criminalise conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' (up to 3 years) and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies (up to 4 years), raise the minimum age for gender-affirming healthcare from 18 to 25 with a permanent-infertility mandate, and expose patients (up to 3 years) and providers (up to 7 years) to charges; the 2025 national monitoring report recorded 6 right-to-life violations (3 hate-motivated killings), 89 torture/ill-treatment violations (51 in 2024), 313 liberty violations with 299 detention decisions, and public-institution 'Year of the Family' directives driving rainbow-symbol bans and expression violations rising from 216 to 540.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (29 October 2025): the leaked 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' (up to 3 years) and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies (up to 4 years); raise the minimum age for gender-affirming healthcare from 18 to 25 with a permanent-infertility mandate and government-hospital evaluations; and enable charges against patients (up to 3 years) and providers (up to 7 years); 15 LGBTI+ groups and the national medical association protested; the European Court of Human Rights' Bayev v Russia precedent is cited as making such amendments incompatible with the human-rights convention.

Kaos GL (24 February 2026): presentation of its LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025, titled 'The Year of the Family: A Major Siege' — in 2025 hostility became explicit state policy (presidency-centred directives, the family ministry as implementing body, religious-broadcast censorship, first closure of an LGBTI+ organisation in years); monitoring recorded 6 right-to-life violations (3 hate-motivated killings), 89 torture/ill-treatment violations (51 in 2024), 313 liberty violations with 299 detention decisions, private-life violations rising from 16 to 67 (including obstruction of hormone therapy), 61 movement violations (travel bans), expression violations rising from 216 to 540 with rainbow-symbol bans as a major source, 336 assembly violations and 40 association violations.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (JS-rendered page, only navigation recovered); the source documents a 31 July 2025 mass ID-check roundup in which police detained trans women, recorded their names and videos, and gave no official reason for detention — detainees called it 'profiling'.

records.name: Antioquia
records.current_summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): Antioquia (incl. Medellín and Bello): by a wide margin the country's most lethal department for LGBTIQ people. Regional evidence: 45 of the 270 LGBTIQ+ killings recorded nationally in 2025 occurred here; the director of Caribe Afirmativo presented the department as one of the most dangerous for LGBTIQ+ people in the country; reporting covering part of the year states that more than half of the country's murders of this population took place in the department, three of them in the municipality of Bello. Emblematic case: Sara Millerey González Borja, 32, a trans woman, beaten and thrown into a creek in Bello on 4 April 2025 while onlookers filmed her; she died of her injuries, triggering vigils and a national alert about rising transfeminicides. No institutional protection finding for Antioquia appears in the monitoring reports - the framing is prejudice, violence and impunity. Scored relative to the national score (0.52) for Colombia.

sources.claim: El País in English (April 14, 2025): on the transphobic murder that shocked Colombia - Sara Millerey, 32, a trans woman, beaten in Bello, Antioquia on 4 April 2025 and thrown into a creek where onlookers filmed her drowning; she died of her injuries; the case was the third LGBTQ murder in Bello that year (the first two victims were gay men); national context: 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025, presidential call to investigate, protests in several cities.

The Guardian (July 30, 2024): 'We are killed for what we are' - trans women in Colombia targeted by armed groups; more than 40 transgender women killed in 2023 (41 recorded), eight between February and April 2024; in Caqueta armed groups circulated flyers announcing a 'social cleansing' against trans women, with remnants of the former largest rebel group still operating despite the 2016 peace agreement; national armed-group threat context.

records.name: Hauts-de-France
records.current_summary: Region research direction: worse than national — municipal practice of the far-right party in the Nord/Pas-de-Calais mining basin. Around thirty local associations accuse newly won far-right town halls of cancelling or hollowing out local Pride events while claiming to defend LGBT rights ("we are not fooled by this pinkwashing"); party MEPs have voted against conversion-therapy resolutions. Documented pattern across several communes, not one mayor's statement. Model-estimate residual (route 3, best-knowledge delta): large urban student scene around Lille vs rural voting patterns inland. National context from this record's sources: trans detainees in French prisons are placed by the gender on their identity documents (criminal procedure code D248), fall into a legal grey area and are punished beyond their alleged crimes — the national detention controller-general's office says transgender detainees are the group that "suffers the most" in detention; its 2021 Opinion covering all places of deprivation of liberty (based on ~40 referrals since 2010) finds serious violations persisting, with isolation, untrained staff and unimplemented 2016 depathologisation identified as the structural causes.

sources.claim: Investigative feature (Jan 2018) on transgender women in French prisons: by law, placement follows the gender on identity documents (criminal procedure code Article D248), so trans women legally marked male are held in all-male facilities — case of Paola, three days in a men's facility near Lille after transfer in 2014, shouted at and threatened by inmates; case of Kara B. held under notorious conditions after a 2016 Paris protest trial; the national detention controller-general (CGLPL) states transgender detainees are the group that "suffers the most" in prison.

National detention controller-general's Opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in all places of deprivation of liberty: serious violations persist across institutions (based on ~40 referrals since 2010 plus interviews and inspections); recommends that detained people choose the gender of their search officer and ward, no isolation because of trans identity, no dedicated trans-only wards, and ongoing hormone/medical care; extends to intersex and non-binary people; notes the 2016 depathologising law has not been translated into prison rules.

records.name: Occitanie
records.current_summary: Region research direction: worse than national — one cancelled Pride, and the one department with a measured above-average offence rate. (1) 13 June 2026: the Pride march in Béziers was cancelled because no volunteers could be found to staff its security — organisers: "we're talking about freedom, about love, about a space where you can be whoever you want" — in a city governed by a mayor whose record of bending public-space rules for conservative ends is separately documented (a human-rights league asked the new préfète to enforce the 1905 law after municipal Hanukkah ceremonies).
